segments.text: Hello everyone, this is Frank Defratis, and welcome to HoloTalk for the week of January 25th, 1999.

A rather short show this week as I've been in the lab with laser pointer holography testing in the evenings and have spent a great deal of time this week looking to see how far back laser pointer holography goes.
My curiosity was piqued going through two books.
Number one Practical Holography by Graham Saxby, and the other book being Homemade Holograms by John Iavini.
In Saxby's Practical Holography, he states on page 38.
If the astigmatism of this beam is corrected by means of optics, a spatially coherent beam can be obtained.
And this has been used experimentally for making holograms, though so far not to any extent outside of the Soviet Union, which of course is now Russia.
Amazingly enough, the papers listed in the reference at the end of the chapter are from 1974, 1976, and 1980.
All of them are from Russia.
If you'd like more information on the paper, send me an email and I'll send you the authors, titles, descriptions, and publications.
In homemade holograms on page 166, we find the following.
Power output is 3.4 milliwatts, and the cost is $575 as of January 1990.
The coherency length of the diode isn't known, but it has been used by a few American holographers to produce holograms.
So I called Bill Arkin at Holo Spectra this week and he did confirm the information.
He couldn't recall offhand who the holographers were, but did mention TJ at Lake Forest as one person who was experimenting with diode holography.
I went through all of my back issues of HoloSphere from the mid-1980s to the time that they ceased publication and could not find any information, although the issues may have been too early.
I also checked Wavefront Holographics International but didn't find anything there either.
This week I'll try to go through my copies of holography news and see if any company released a report on working with diodes.
So there has to be news and a history out there.
If you have worked with diodes to create holograms or know of someone who was within the last 10 years, please contact me so we can get a nice background of information together on this.
First time on Saturday evening, March 6th, at the Central New Jersey Mensa Conference held at the Holiday Inn at Tinekan Falls, New Jersey.
I will be the keynote speaker for the event.
So if you're in the area, come out and be one of the first people to see these images.
I'll have a web page on the event within the next week.
And also, Hollow Talk will be recorded live during the event and will be the program for the week of March 15th, so stay tuned for more information on this.
Steve Michael sent in a report this week.
He's been working with Kodak Film for making his laser pointer holograms and has had some success.
Here is his email which I will read to you.
I just made a bright transmission with Kodak SO 2535, equivalent in brightness to 8E75, which is AGFA.
It has an exposure rating of 5 ergs per square centimeter for a density of 1, and my exposure time was 3 seconds with a beam intensity reading at the film holder of 1.7 microwatts.
The laser pointer was producing 2.45 milliwatts undiverged.
Because of the antihalation backing, I threw in rapid fixer between the stop bath and bleach, and it worked beautifully.
Cost of the film is about $2.50 per sheet.
Now I will try a reflection, but I am still trying to remove the anti-halation backing prior to exposure.
Kodak's suggestion didn't work, which was 80 degree water with a 2 to 5% acetic acid bath.
Kodak says there's nothing special in the fixer that removes the backing, but I know that's not true since I can see the backing vanish rapidly using fixer.
I have a good idea what component it is and will experiment today on that aspect.
And I will keep you posted on further updates from Steve and his work.
Now I had a group of students come in from the New York area to learn about how to make holograms using a laser pointer.
And after the workshop, we sat down in the studio and recorded a few of their impressions and ideas on holography in general.
It's always good to hear from the upcoming generation, and it will be them that we will pass the torch on to in the future.
Here are a few audio clips from our conversations.
And we have Michael, Brittany, Samantha, and Mom Joan.
I'll be back right after they're finished.
Would you like to make your own one-of-a-kind hologram and learn how you can start making holograms on your own at the same time?
You can do this and much more by attending one of Frank the Fraytest's holography workshops.
From beginner to advance, Frank's got a workshop that's just right for you.
From single afternoon, evening or weekend introductory workshops to Wednesday evening five-week complete courses.
And don't forget his newest workshop, Laser Pointer Holography.
Located just off the northeast extension of the Pennsylvania Turnpike and Interstate 78.
The studio is a quick non-stop drive from the New York, Philadelphia, and Baltimore, Washington, D.C.
areas.
